Mini-Conference Theme: Petro- versus Electrostates? Global and domestic struggles over green energy transitions

We live through a critical moment in green energy transitions globally. In the past years, the adoption of renewables has accelerated, mainly thanks to Chinese industrial policy. Many countries, particularly in Europe, have now entered advanced power sector transitions, generating more than half of their electricity from wind and sun. But challenges to these transitions remain unexpectedly high. Donald Trump aims to entrench the United States as a primary petro-state and has reversed the green push of the Inflation Reduction Act. European leaders have committed to support this project by buying extraordinary volumes of US hydrocarbons, in exchange for favorable trade terms. Chinese renewables buildout and electrification are record-breaking. But the country continues to consume huge volumes of fossil energy – domestic coal as well as oil and gas imported from the very states (U.S., Russia, Saudi Arabia) that spearhead a global anti-decarbonization alliance. European leaders in renewables also face domestic challenges: Soaring energy prices related to oil and gas during the Russia-Ukraine and Iran wars; problems of integrating new energy sources with existing grid management; and the strengthening of anti-decarbonization forces on the extreme right. Emerging economies, from Brazilian re-invention of modern renewable energy auctions, Ethiopia’s Grand Renaissance Dam hope to power an entire continental region, or Vietnam’s bold bet on offshore wind energy, constitute political projects to transform economies through energy, generating their own domestic and international struggles.

Energy has always been a critical topic for socio-economics but continues to remain weakly integrated into our understandings of (geo-)political as well as capitalist change. For instance, much of the geopolitics literature is on oil but very little has been written about the geopolitical implications of renewable electrification. Recent literature on domestic energy politics concentrates on conflicts around renewable technologies but little research addresses system-level issues (grids etc.). In the SASE context, these topics sit uncomfortably between several networks and remain underrepresented (also within SER). Aspects are covered in sessions on regulation, comparative capitalism, and in discussions on climate change/policy. But the SASE community has not given sustained attention to the radical transformations of energy systems experienced during our times and the deep international as well as domestic conflicts revolving around them. We see a strong demand for exploring intersections between domestic and global changes in energy and the multi-level conflicts revolving around them. Material interests, but also international networks of expertise, financing regimes, investment protection practices, and ideational change need to be explored as possible factors shaping these transitions and conflicts.

Recently, colleagues have proposed an integrative perspective by juxtaposing petro- against electro-states: the former – the US, Saudi Arabia, Russia - entrenching fossil dependencies, the latter – most notably China – rapidly transitioning to renewables at home while forging trade relations around green tech, in particular with Europe. However, these ideas of international energy realignments remain poorly developed. For instance, the supposed electro-regimes in China and Europe continue to foster fossil relationships while experiencing new challenges for renewables expansion and electrification at home. New resource dependencies emerge over critical minerals. The United States may be pivoting to hydrocarbon exports, but its model of domestic consumption-led growth, let alone its project of reindustrialization, stand in contradiction with these aims (reflected recently in the Iran war-related inflationary surge). These contradictions parallel domestic politics struggles, as exemplified in Canada’s or Brazil’s hydro versus oil wealth regimes. Labor relations and the role of industry conglomerates should feature more prominently in the literature.

The organizers thus think the time is ripe for the SASE community to dedicate a mini-conference to conflicts around rapidly transforming energy systems that can be observed domestically as well as internationally. This mini-conference would help to bring regular SASE scholars from different networks together with researchers who usually present work in other venues. The topic is complementary to, but does not fully overlap with other networks. Cross-listings could be made with networks E, H, L, and S.

Indicative panel themes:

Different transition speeds or true divergence?

A first panel theme revolves around the question of whether the notion of ongoing green transitions with different speeds still holds, or whether we observe a true divergence between accelerated expansion of renewables in some regions and significant slowdown in others, leading to divergent energy systems, political economies, and climate regimes.

Foreign energy interests versus domestic decarbonization

Do countries’ energy interests towards other countries align or conflict with domestic energy and climate policy interests? Mechanisms of convergence exist, e.g. when export-oriented green tech sector lobby for domestic renewables deployment and electrification. However, we can also see divergent pathways, e.g. when countries join green value chains without incentives for domestic decarbonization.

Grid integration conflicts

In the process of expanding renewables, many countries and regions plan to build larger and often cross-national grids in order to deal with intermittency and to increase energy security. Examples of this are the European common market project, China’s Global Energy Interconnection, North American grid integration, and the unfinished project of a Central American grid. However, these projects raise conflicts over infrastructure costs, the effects on energy prices, and over different ideologies, pitting local self-sufficiency/autonomy against international cooperation.

States or markets in coordinating system overhaul

The early phases of renewables expansions in Europe and the US have been shaped by a combination of liberalization plus technology support policies; the respective countries now face an abundance of project- and decades-long interconnection queues. When centralized planning has occurred, they have remained private or outside the scope of public scrutiny. By contrast, Chinese renewables buildout has been state-driven, though coordination between various provinces and state-owned companies has remained complex. In advanced transitions, system overhaul becomes increasingly pressing. An increasingly relevant meta-conflict concerns the role of the state or markets in accomplishing such high-level coordination.

Industrial reorganization struggles around power

Geographical size of the optimal power grids matters in shaping energy-manufacturing co-location, the resilience and complexity of grid management, and the extent of necessary system overhaul. Questions of “engineering” design converge with industrial policy and the organization of the electric power sector. Examples include China’s “zero-carbon industrial-park” initiative, Pakistan’s rapid expansion of rooftop solar, and the deployment of renewable-powered data-centers. These developments reduce sub-national dependencies on traditional utilities and reshape domestic energy politics and “geographical” politics by shifting decision-making authority toward regional or corporate owners of microgrid infrastructure.

Mini-Conference Theme: The New Politics of Derisking: Reconstruction, Resilience, and Hope

16-18 June, 2027 | Online

By placing derisking at the centre of analysis, the mini-conference addresses both the possibilities and the limits of contemporary reconstruction efforts. It considers how current and historically comparable practices of risk allocation may stabilise investment while entrenching unequal distributions of power and exposure. It also engages with emerging attempts to reconfigure risk sharing through institutional innovation at multiple scales, including municipal initiatives, public financial institutions and transnational forms of coordination.

Finally, it considers how derisking reshapes global production networks, strategic industries, and cross-border investment, creating opportunities for some regions and dependencies for others. In doing so, this mini-conference introduces a perspective that remains relatively underrepresented within SASE, namely a systematic focus on derisking as a governing logic of contemporary and long-run capitalism and as a terrain of political contestation in processes of reconstruction. This builds on the successful mini-conference on derisking held at SASE 2026. The current proposal reframes derisking as a contested instrument of creative reconstruction and institutional rebuilding in a moment of disruption, while the 2026 version presented derisking as a political project reshaping state-market relations and global hierarchies.

Key questions

  • How is derisking being mobilised in efforts to reconstruct economic institutions, productive capacity, and public infrastructure?
  • What institutional and financial architectures underpin derisking, what liabilities do they create, and how are these funded?
  • How does derisking reshape global production, strategic industries, foreign investment, and economic dependencies across states and regions?
  • How are risks, returns, costs, and governing authority distributed across states, firms, workers, communities, and territories in either the current or comparative historical context?
  • How do labour, civil society, municipalities, and local communities contest or develop alternatives to dominant derisking arrangements?

Proposed themes

  • Institutional architectures and productive reconstruction. Examines how derisking is embedded in efforts to rebuild state capacity, public infrastructures, strategic industries, and productive capabilities. Contributions may analyse public financial institutions, guarantees, revenue commitments, industrial policy instruments, and other arrangements through which investment is enabled and governed.
  • Geopolitics, economic security, and uneven development. Analyses how derisking shapes responses to geopolitical fragmentation, trade conflict, supply chain disruption, and economic security concerns. It considers regionalisation, friend-shoring, global production networks, and the uneven distribution of productive capacities and dependencies across regions and between the Global North and South.
  • Finance, distribution, and democratic accountability. Investigates how derisking redistributes risks and returns, creates public and private liabilities, and allocates costs across states, firms, organised labour, and communities. This theme includes work on financialisation, corporate concentration, public guarantees, labour, social protection, and the democratic governance of long-term financial commitments.
  • Contestation and alternative forms of risk-sharing. Explores how labour organisations, civil society, municipalities, and local communities contest or rework dominant derisking arrangements. It also examines alternatives such as public banking, cooperative ownership, municipal industrial strategies, mutualised finance, and other institutional arrangements intended to embed investment within more accountable and socially oriented forms of governance.

Mini-Conference Theme: Who builds the Transition? Trade Unions, Worker Power, and Ecological Reconstruction

The ecological transition is unfolding amid profound disruptions to both work and the institutions through which workers have historically exercised collective power. Climate impacts are intensifying as resurgent reactionary right-wing and ethno-nationalist leaders and their movements, increasing militarization, much of which is funded and enabled by new technologies of machine production and surveillance (Henaway 2023). Each of these trends, in ways both great and small, worsens both local and global environmental conditions. Meanwhile, many of the institutions and policies that were expected to underpin a transition toward low-carbon economies, including green industrial policy, public investment, and international climate cooperation are contested, weakened, or redirected. Yet, moments like these can create openings for rebuilding institutions, solidarities, and relations of production. With that backdrop, labour environmentalism must not only consider how workers and trade unions respond to ecological transition but what role they can play in reconstructing its alternatives.

Take for instance the notion of “just transition”. The original notion of a just transition, advanced by Tony Mazzochi, was that just like an environmental superfund, so too should there be one for workers (Leopold 2007). Mazzochi’s vision, however, was arguably much broader and ambitious in scope than much of how “just transition” is often invoked by both scholars and policy makers today. The emphasis on the simple one-to-one replacement of carbon-intensive jobs with new ones, often of marginal quality, winnows down the political horizon of labour environmentalism. Of course, the notion of a just transition is not the only idea advanced by labour environmentalists. New strategies for collective bargaining, public ownership proposals, worker cooperatives, sectoral planning, industrial policy, community-labour coalitions, migrant worker organizations, reforms to the working day, and other eco-social political economic arrangements for alternative forms of living also feature. All the while, each political potential must grapple with the tension of who is or is not recognized as a “worker” in the pursuit of these policies (Barca 2024; Akbulut, 2024). And, relatedly, how can solidarities and resonances between workers be appreciated with both breadth and depth? Finally, do these alternatives help build power to make change possible?

This also requires critical attention to who constitutes the worker within broader socio-ecological transition politics. Labor movements themselves are internally differentiated by migration status, race, gender, citizenship, occupation, geography, and uneven access to collective representation. Michael Denning’s concept of “wageless life” offers a productive intervention to re-imagining labor struggles within socio-ecological transitions. Denning argues that analyses of capitalism should not begin with the employment contract, but with the dispossession that produces the imperative to earn a living in the first place. The proletarian, in this account, is not just the wage laborer but the person made radically dependent upon the market for subsistence. Employment is therefore not universal, nor secure. Workers continually confront the possibility that capital will have no use for their labor. This perspective complicates familiar narratives of Just Transition. If ecological reconstruction is imagined primarily through the creation of “green jobs,” what happens to those whose labor is informal, unwaged, reproductive, intermittently employed, or rendered surplus through economic and technological restructuring?

For SASE 2027, submissions are encouraged that engage labor environmentalism and the question of: how can workers rebuild the foundations of socio-economic systems so that the majority of people’s’ ability to live is decoupled from capital’s mute compulsion (see Mau 2023)? Organized by the Trade Unions and Labour Environmentalism (TULE), a cross-national and interdisciplinary network foregrounding the role and function of labour in socio-ecological transitions. Prospective papers are invited that engage with the themes and/or questions outlined below, with an emphasis on direct engagement with the workplace (broadly construed), communities, and/or sectoral case studies.

  • Is employment creation an adequate horizon for Just Transition, and what would ecological reconstruction beyond the wage look like?
  • How does the enclosure, dispossession and wagelessness underlying capitalist labour markets shape workers’ capacity to contest environmentally destructive industries?
  • How might Just Transition and/or other frameworks commit to socio-ecological transitions account for the unemployed, informal, migrant, seasonal, precarious, and reproductive and subsistence workers? And what forms of solidarity can connect them to organized labour?
  • What labour-led alternatives and experiments can advance social and ecological well-being? (e.g., bargaining for the common good, community-labour coalitions etc.,)
  • What are the implications of ecological restructuring for transnational and emerging “green sector” labour forces, and what does worker power look like when stable employment is no longer its presumed foundation?
  • What does a labour led eco-social politics look like and how might it be scaled?
  • Reflections on “doing” labour environmentalism including participatory, worker-led comparative, historical, and other methodological approaches.

These questions speak directly to SASE 2027’s call to examine efforts to “rebuild key institutional and political formations” amid disruption and to learn from experiments capable of promoting shared prosperity and democracy. They also build upon TULE’s ongoing commitment to foregrounding trade unions and organized labour within environmental labour studies while remaining critically attentive to the contradictions and limitations of organized labour itself, including its own historically uneven engagement with gender and social reproduction. By bringing together research across sectors, countries, and disciplinary transitions, this mini conference asks what labour environmentalism can contribute not merely towards managing ecological transition, but to reconstructing economies around different relations between work, nature, democracy, and collective life. At a moment when existing institutions are being dismantled and ecological crises deepen; the challenge is not to defend what remains but to build in its place

Mini-Confernce Theme: Financial subordination and alternative pathways: limits of reform, possibilities for transformation

Recent decades have witnessed the deepening integration of economies into a global financial system characterised by persistent asymmetries of power, uneven access to credit and liquidity, hierarchical monetary arrangements, and unequal patterns of development. The concept of international financial subordination has emerged as a valuable framework for understanding how these asymmetries shape the developmental trajectories of countries, regions, firms, and social groups. By highlighting the structural constraints imposed by the international monetary and financial system, financial subordination sheds light on the ways in which financial hierarchies reproduce economic dependency, vulnerability to crises, and unequal opportunities for growth and social transformation.

At the same time, the contemporary global economy is experiencing profound disruptions. Escalating geopolitical tensions, climate change, technological transformations, recurrent financial crises, and the reconfiguration of global value chains have intensified debates about the future of globalisation and the institutional foundations of economic development. In this context, established assumptions regarding financial governance, development strategies, and international economic cooperation are being challenged. New initiatives, institutions, and policy experiments have emerged, while calls for economic sovereignty, development alternatives, and more democratic forms of economic coordination have gained renewed prominence.

This mini-conference seeks to explore the analytical and political implications of financial subordination in this changing context. In particular, it aims to address a central question: does recognising financial subordination point towards pragmatic reconstruction within existing capitalist institutions, or does it reveal the limits of reform and the need for more radical forms of economic and social transformation?

The mini-conference invites contributions that engage with financial subordination as a framework for understanding contemporary capitalism and for identifying alternative pathways for development. It is particularly interested in dialogue across heterodox traditions, including post-Keynesian, Marxian, dependency, structuralist, institutionalist, feminist, ecological, and decolonial approaches. In line with SASE's commitment to pluralism and its interest in underrepresented perspectives, the mini-conference also encourages contributions from and about the Global South, as well as work addressing race, ethnicity, migration, and other dimensions of uneven development.

Possible themes include, but are not limited to:

  • Financial subordination, dependency, and uneven development;
  • Monetary hierarchies, currency internationalisation, and global liquidity;
  • The political economy of economic sovereignty and policy space;
  • Financialisation and the reproduction of inequalities across countries and regions;
  • Financial subordination and the production of inequalities across class, gender, race, and space;
  • Climate change, green transitions, and sustainable development under conditions of financial subordination;
  • Technological change, digital finance, and new forms of dependency and exclusion;South-South cooperation and alternative financial architectures;
  • Geopolitical realignments, multipolarity, and the future of the international monetary system;
  • The role of development banks, industrial policy, and public investment in overcoming financial constraints;
  • Feminist, decolonial, and anti-racist perspectives on financial hierarchies and development;Historical and contemporary experiences of resistance, reform, and transformation.

By bringing together scholars from diverse disciplinary and theoretical backgrounds, the mini- conference aims to advance debates on the causes, consequences, and future of financial subordination. Beyond diagnosing contemporary challenges, it seeks to examine how alternative institutions, development strategies, and collective political projects might contribute to rebuilding the economic foundations necessary for more equitable, sustainable, and hopeful futures. In doing so, the mini-conference directly engages with the broader conference theme by asking how societies can move beyond entrenched forms of dependency and inequality and create new possibilities for development in a moment of global disruption.

Network Q Theme: Remaking Asian Capitalisms – New Paths of Development in Times of Disruption

Please find the general SASE 2027 entry here.

Network Q promotes theory and research on the diversity of socio-economic systems and capitalist development in Asia as well as its global implications. The network welcomes a wide range of theoretical perspectives (e.g. comparative and international political economy, economic sociology, management studies, industrial sociology, innovation studies, political science and international relations, geography, development studies, anthropology).

Across Asia, governments, firms, workers and communities are seeking to explore new paths of development amid geopolitical tension, technological change and climate disruption. Debates over industrial policy, energy transitions, labour rights and social protection ask not only how economies can adapt, but who directs reconstruction, who bears its costs and whether it can support more secure livelihoods.

Development is increasingly an intra-Asian process. Investment, supply chains, technology, energy and labour migration connect Asian economies, but not on equal terms. As production and strategic industries are reorganised, established centres may gain new forms of influence, while emerging manufacturing and resource-producing economies may gain opportunities without gaining equivalent control over technology, finance or value. These shifts may reproduce, unsettle or create new centre–periphery relationships within Asia.

While China remains a magnet for debates on Asian Capitalisms, to reflect on these dynamics, we particularly welcome work on and from South and Southeast Asia. We also seek to expand the presentation of work on Japan and South Korea.

Network Q also seeks to bring detailed knowledge of Asian economies and regions into dialogue with broader debates in political economy. The network welcomes contributions that use area expertise to develop, challenge or refine theories of capitalism, development, institutional change and global political economy.

The network welcomes papers and panels addressing, inter alia:

  • Industrial policy and the building and rebuilding of productive capacity.
  • Changing relationships among states, firms, workers and communities within structural change.
  • Intra-Asian investment, trade, finance and production networks.
  • Shifting centres and peripheries within Asia: who controls technology, captures value and carries risk?
  • The prospects and limits of economic self-reliance, strategic autonomy and regional cooperation.
  • The political economy energy security, climate adaptation, and green transitions.
  • Digital infrastructure, platforms, AI and semiconductor policy.
  • Labour migration, workers’ organising, wages, and skills in transnational Asian capitalism.
  • Urban and rural development, including uneven access to infrastructure and investment.
  • Contestation and resistance across Asian capitalisms.

For the 2027 conference, Network Q invites individual paper submissions, submissions for thematic panels, and SASE Book Salon panels on recently published books. Abstracts should be no longer than 1,000 words (plus references).

Thematic panels can address any themes and issues related to the aims and scope of the network and should be based on paper drafts with a structured discussion including a discussant. Book Salon panels consist of a book author, a chair/moderator, and a maximum of four discussants with relevant expertise on a recently published book speaking to Network Q themes. Note that SASE seeks to promote gender equality. We thus strongly encourage you to take gender balance into account in panel proposals.

Submissions should be done through the SASE website.

Please send your abstracts by 1st November 2026 (approx. 1,000 words)

As part of the mini-conference, the organizers will host one virtual session during the virtual conference days (16th-18th June 2027). There will be no hybrid sessions during the on-site conference.

item.title: A World of a Thousand Cuts: Forests, Wood, and Industrialisation across the Globe in the 19th and 20th Centuries (Turin, July 2027)
item.description:
Deadline: 15 June 2027

6-8 July 2027 | Turin, Italy

The mainstream historiographies of industrialisation habitually emphasise the novel energy sources and materials that powered this transformative era, such as coal, steel, steam and electricity, implicitly assuming that wood, an important pre-industrial resource, was destined for an inevitable decline. Histories of industrialisation also disproportionately focus on Europe and North America. Stemming from the research vectors of the ERC Starting Grant “Industrial Wood: European Industrialisation as Seen from the Forests (1870-1914)”, this conference aims to rethink the relevance of wood in an unevenly industrialising world throughout the 19th and 20th centuries. It follows more recent interpretative paths, which draw attention to the material diversity of industrial metabolism, in order to achieve a more complex understanding of the social, economic and environmental histories of industrialisation. The conference also seeks to geographically decentre the research perspective and discover the links between forests and industrialisation in the global context.

Industrialisation, understood as a systemic social and economic transformation underpinned by technological innovations and leading to changes in production regimes, was an uneven and chronologically mis-aligned process within Europe and globally, stretching from the late 18th century far into the 20th century. Consequently, the relationship between industrialisation and forest exploitation varied depending on the national and international politics, markets, law regulations, access to technology, environmental movements, property and labour regimes, imperial dynamics and colonial power. Attentive to these complexities, the organisers have approached industrialisation as an a-synchronous, multi-focal and globally encompassing social and economic process, activated by a confluence of economic impetus and political agenda.

Even if in the course of industrialisation wood has been marginalised as a combustible, it maintained its significance in industrial economies as a construction material. Moreover, innovations in technology and transportation – both the drivers and the outcomes of industrialisation – made forests increasingly accessible for large-scale extraction, thus bringing industrial logging into the furthest reaches of the woods and fundamentally reshaping them economically, socially and ecologically. Recent historical, anthropological and archeological studies, focusing mostly on North America and Europe, show that extractivism, (im)migration and environmental degradation were a part of this process. They also reveal that industrialisation of timber production did not mean a complete break with rural economies, and that the demand for wood as fuel or production material (for paper or packaging, for example) changes depending on the historical moment. Through this conference, we aim to broaden the conversation geographically to include global histories of industrialisation and to answer these questions: how did industrialisation change the world’s forests? What kinds of new relationships, dependencies and hierarchies did the arrival of industrialisation within the forest context instigate with regards to natural environments and the working lives linked to their transformation? How does our understanding of industrialisation change when we cease to read it as a sequence of substitutions and instead view it as a process of persistence, accumulation and re-articulation, wherein old material and energy flows are not erased by new ones but are intricately woven into them, undergoing profound transformation? Ultimately, what does the industrialisation of forests mean? And how do we adjust our research methodologies to answer these questions?

The conference seeks to explore cases, with a double focus on forests and industrialisation, in various political contexts and across different geographies throughout the 19th and 20th centuries. The papers should relate to but do not have to be limited to the following themes:

  • industrialisation and wood consumption
  • labour, migration, gender and ethnicity
  • empires, colonialism and decolonisation
  • industrial wood uses, wood-based businesses and geographies of timber flow
  • networks, circulation of ideas and technology
  • industrial timberscapes (timber production complexes, workers settlements, infrastructure)
  • deindustrialisation and its impact on livelihoods
  • environmental effects of industrialisation in forests

Scholars in humanities and social sciences, interested in these topics, are welcome to apply. Ultimately, the conference aims to foster an interdisciplinary confluence between environmental history, social history, economic history, environmental anthropology and related sub-disciplines. We invite contributions from doctoral students, post-doctoral researchers and senior scholars.

Conference theme: Critical Management Studies beyond the Academy?

It seems that the legitimation crises of the University and the Academy are a recurrent feature of modernity (or late- or post- modernity). Today, this question presses with a particular urgency. The university has come to appear simultaneously as an institution estranged from a unifying sense of public purpose, organised under increasingly vacant terms of legitimation and accountability – “excellence”, “student experience”, “research impact”, “knowledge exchange”, “graduate employability/outcomes”. It has become subjected to the remorseless disciplines of managerial neoliberalisation, marketisation, and hierarchical bureaucratic authority; and to ‘competition’ by commercialised forms of dissemination and algorithmically-legitimated simulacra of epistemic claims. These present crises, then, appear to ostensibly concern precisely the foreclosure of this question: as the university’s purposes are increasingly homogenised by the vacuous language of managerialism, its constitutive relation to the wider social worlds beyond its institutional boundaries becomes more pressing than ever. This is despite long-standing critical work showing that the Academy and academic work and labour more broadly, is always implicated in the institutions, communities, struggles, and material conditions it helps to shape (see, for example Boussebaa, 2020; Cunliffe and Pavlovich, 2022; Goddard et al., 2016; Goddard and Vallance, 2013; Parker, 2023; Smith, 2008; Zanoni et al., 2025).

Building on these tensions as points of consolidation and departure, the organizers seek to stimulate and explore how the ideas and concepts pursued within Critical Management Studies (CMS) and allied disciplines are experienced and played out in the communities, workplaces and social spaces beyond the ‘standard’ sites of academic practice (Butler et al., 2018; Fleming and Banerjee, 2016; King and Land, 2018; Spicer et al., 2009). The organizers also seek to enquire into what other modes of epistemic production may be caring, or generative for practice, research and/or theory (Antoni and Beer, 2024; Bartunek and Lei, 2026), as well as critiquing the reproduction of the ‘Academy’ and the politics of particular forms of epistemic production and dissemination (Boussebaa, 2020; Muzanenhamo and Chowdhury, 2023; Parker, 2023; Prasad and Śliwa, 2024; Santos, 2012).

The organizers welcome submissions for streams, sessions, workshops, panels, ideas, proposals, epistemic forays and other fora or activities which address or problematise the primary question of “What relations are there (or should there be?) between the forms of organising that are conceptualised, critiqued and encouraged in academic writing and research and the world beyond the Academy?” For example, are these forms of organising imaginable, possible, infectious, realisable, resonant, transmissible, reworked, discordant, resisted, liveable, mimetic, translatable, rendered untenable and/or generative beyond the Academy?. In posing this primary question, we encourage critical scrutiny of potential assumptions and biases inherent within it – whether prefiguring beyond as refusal, reworking, a mode of surpassing, co-witnessing or co-production. Secondarily, we also seek critical engagements with the constriction, assault upon, precariatisation and restructuring of the Academy in many parts of the world, and the institutionalised and commercialised processes of academic publication and dissemination. Likewise, we also encourage creative excursions in critical management studies and allied disciplines, for example, in terms of different modes of epistemic engagement, co-production or reception.

The organizers also encourage streams that reflect and inquire into the following, including but not limited to:

  • The broad range of critical management studies topics – for example, labour process theory; labour regime theory, critical global value chain research; critical accounting studies; critical finance studies; critical entrepreneurship studies; critical leadership studies; critical marketing studies; heterodox and ecological economics; critical management education and pedagogical studies; critical studies of innovation; critical diversity studies;
  • Crossovers and conversations with other allied disciplines and topic areas where the phenomenon of management entails critical questioning – for example, critical political ecology; sociology and cultural studies; public and social policy and administration; discard/waste studies; gender studies; decolonial/postcolonial studies; media and communication studies; critical legal studies; critical governance studies; science and technology studies; critical discourse studies; critical psychological and/or psychodynamic studies;
  • The temporal, geographic, and cultural diversity of forms of managing and organising, and how they are conceptualised or constructed, for example, studies from within or about Latin America, Africa, South-East Asia, Oceania, amongst other regions of the world, and indeed, outer space;
  • Types of interventionist research, engagement or pedagogy with a critical or emancipatory intent – for example, critical action research, activity theory, co-design research, the pedagogy of the oppressed.

Submissions are now open for streams, sessions, workshops, panels, ideas and proposals which could include (but are not limited to):

  • Paper presentations
  • Critical Development Workshops (including research community, paper development, or professional development)
  • Activist Workshops
  • Public Engagement Workshops, Lectures, or Panels
  • Exhibitions, Installations, Creative Sessions, Events or other interventions (e.g. music, poetry, storytelling, nature-based rambles, guided discussions or social gatherings, participatory practices etc)
  • Other proposals beyond the above

This should not be considered as a comprehensive or restrictive list, and the organizers would welcome all submissions that creatively embody critical management studies and/or practices in form and/or content.

item.title: Workshop: From the Origin to the Future of Money (Linz, March 2027)
item.description:
Deadline: 10 December 2026

31 March - 2 April, 2027 | Linz, Austria

Workshop theme: From the Origin to the Future of Money

Institute of Philosophy and Scientific Method (JKU Linz, Austria)

Political and scientific debates about the future of money are often underpinned by diverging accounts of money’s origin. This pattern appears to be relatively stable in the history of monetary theory. Carl Menger put forward an explanation of the spontaneous emergence of money as a market phenomenon which is invoked by later members of the Austrian School in their argumentation against state intervention in the monetary system. Georg Friedrich Knapp described money as a “creature of the legal order”; Alfred Mitchell-Innes understood money as credit. Both inspired post-Keynesians and proponents of MMT to advocate for the active construction and management of monetary systems. Karl Marx based his rejection of monetary reform on his view of money as a necessary feature of capitalism which, if abolished, would spontaneously re-originate.

How to best make sense of the connection between descriptive accounts of the origin of money and normative proposals for the future of money? Do investigations into money’s origin allow insights about its “essential nature” which, in turn, has normative implications? Are positions regarding the origin, nature, and politics of money as well as the proper method of investigation embedded in distinct worldviews? Or is the supposed connection merely a result of naturalist fallacies and strategic attempts at persuasion?

Addressing these interdisciplinary questions requires joint efforts by philosophers, economists, and historians. This workshop aims to facilitate such fruitful interaction and cooperation. Topics for submission include but are not limited to:

  • Development of different schools of monetary theory and their interaction
  • Comparing and evaluating theories of the origin of money
  • “What is money”: essentialism vs. nominalism
  • Descriptive and normative aspects of monetary theory
  • Discretionary vs. rule-based monetary policy
  • Contemporary proposals for the future of money (cryptocurrencies, CBDC, MMT, etc.)
  • Methodological individualism and its discontents
  • Methodological problems of different price indices (CPI, OOHPI, …)
  • Worldviews and adversarial collaboration

Abstracts should be 300-400 words (including references, if needed) and be submitted via e-mail to Jakob Gschwandtner, in an editable format (DOCX, ODT, etc.). All presentations are in person in Linz.

The past decade has witnessed an unprecedented crisis of liberal democracy — in the United States with the rise of Trumpism, and worldwide with the spread of authoritarian politics undergirded by populist and nationalist movements. These developments did not emerge from nowhere: neoliberal policies have generated economic inequality and political polarization on a scale not seen since the Gilded Age, with disastrous consequences for working classes, the poor, and other marginalized social groups. As these conditions have become institutionalized, we are witnessing accelerating attempts to dismantle liberal democracy itself. What is the nature of the new political and economic regime consolidating today? What is its social base of support? And what comes next for the left?

item.title: Conference on "Against, With, and For Artificial Intelligence – the Many Faces of Techno-Resistance" (Malmö, November 2026)
item.description:
Deadline: 1 October 2026

5 November, 2026 | Malmö, Sweden

Conference theme: Against, With, and For Artificial Intelligence – the Many Faces of Techno-Resistance

Polls and pundits frequently tell us that people distrust AI. Yet, governments continue to support AI firms and the value of chipmakers key to AI keeps rising exponentially. Many of the CEOs leading those firms continue to be the poster faces of a supposed fight against the elite yet have themselves had economic power and political influence at the centre of that elite for well over a decade. This one-day conference seeks to open up three seemingly contradictory faces of techno-resistance in the age of AI.

In an otherwise polarised age, ‘Anti-‘ or ‘Alter-AI’ (in various forms) has become the empty signifier of a movement crossing the political spectrum as well as a proxy for wider movements against centralisation. The increasing roll-out of AI in the physical world has been met by anti-robot attacks, people posting videos of their acts and encouraging others to follow suit. Environmentalists are finding new friends as they challenge new datacentres projects. Resistance against AI can also provide a means of feedback for improving real-world use of AI, as well as resistance toward representations of AI, negotiation surrounding AI regulations, and its public use.

Yet, whilst people are seeking to resist against AI, we also see cases of people using AI as a tool to resist other targets. This includes cash-strapped NGOs seeking to compensate for reduced funding but also everyday individuals looking to improve their self-representation when contacting firms, politicians, and their local doctor. For some, utilising AI within so-called ‘civic tech’ opens the door to new and more democratic means for decision-making as well as strengthen communities. Others warn that the political-economic structure behind AI, including who owns the algorithms and data, means it is a fool’s paradise to believe such platforms can bring new energy to the public sphere.

And we should not forget that a key part of the ideological undercurrent within Silicon Valley and its satellites remains a belief that they are developing AI as an alternative to current ways of organising society. From private settlements based on bitcoin to AI-focused religions, the demand for AI serves as a flag held by often extremely wealthy individuals seeking to resist conventional politics based around democracy and public authorities.

Given the many ways one might think about resistance in relationship to AI, the organizers invite for a full-day in-person conference in Malmö, Sweden.

To be considered, please submit an abstract (max 250 words) emailed to the conference main organiser Michael.Strange@mau.se by 1st October 2026 (subject: RESISTANCE-AI). Attendance is free and includes a coffee break and lunch.

Topics

  • Resisting mainstream visualisation of AI
  • Resistance as a source of innovation for better AI
  • Underground extremist movements against AI
  • ‘Anti-AI’ as the umbrella of a wider social movement
  • Tech bro self-narratives as ‘revolutionaries’
  • Civic tech and civil society – the good and bad
  • Conceptualising resistance strategies in AI
  • Contesting AI regulation
  • Resistance across design, development, and deployment of AI
  • Resistance by civil servants
  • Resistance by everyday actors
  • Professional resistance – how workers seek to modify, subvert, and/or avoid AI

The conference is hosted by the Future Society & Democracy in Europe research group kindly funded by the Centre for Modern European Studies, a joint initiative between the University of Copenhagen, Malmö University, and Lund University. In collaboration with the AI Politics Hub, Malmö University.

item.title: Call for Proposals for Special Issues in the Socio-Economic Review
item.description:
Deadline: 30 September 2026

Socio-Economic Review (SER) is pleased to invite proposals for Special Issues to be published in 2027 or 2028.

A Special Issue is a peer reviewed collection of articles on a specific theme. The theme should normally focus on a new or distinctive area of inquiry insufficiently explored in socio-economic literature, has a broad relevance, and falls within the aims and scope of the journal. Thereby, a special issue provides an opportunity to collectively explore a new topic, develop insightful new lines of research and exchange in dialogue across disciplines such as sociology, political science, economics, business, law, or history.

The proposal should contain the following information:

  1. The names, contact details, and positions of the proposed Guest Editors together with brief biographical details.
  2. The title of the proposed special issue.
  3. A one-page Call for Papers indicating the main theme, key topics, and methodological foci for submissions to the Special Issue.
  4. A list containing titles and short abstracts of any potential contributions, information about the authors and indication of their commitment. Guest editors are not permitted to submit regular peer review papers for the special issue but are encouraged to write a substantive introductory article developing the state of the art around the topic.
  5. A description of the behind the proposal, its planned scope, innovative nature in relation to existing published work, and likely relevance for readers of Socio-Economic Review. Please read the Editorial Policy Statement of SER via the following webpage:
  6. An envisioned timetable including a deadline for the first submission, a period for review and resubmission, and deadline for final print-ready papers.

The team of Guest Editors for the Special Issue will handle all manuscripts from their initial submission; they assign reviewers, and they make decisions (reject, revise, conditionally accept) and communicate those decisions to the authors. While Special Issues are always accompanied by an Open Call for Papers, Guest Editors are also encouraged to reach out to potential contributors to solicit quality submissions. All manuscripts for the Special Issue must undergo double-blind peer review and revisions according to normal SER review process and in accordance with SER’s editorial policy and formal guidelines. Final acceptance of papers is done in consultation with the Chief Editors of SER.

A special issue typically has 6-10 regular length papers plus editors’ introduction. SER manuscripts are generally no longer than 10,000 words in length (inclusive of references, but excluding tables, figures, appendices and online appendices). Manuscripts should follow a clear line of argument and be written in a concise style without sacrificing meaningful content.

Proposals and queries may be sent to chief editors Akos Rona-Tas and Alya Guseva.

item.title: Journal of Institutional Economics: Symposium on "The Institutional Foundations of Stakeholder Theory. Insights from Original and Non-Mainstream Institutional Economics"
item.description:
Deadline: 31 January 2027

Stakeholder theory is often presented as an ethical correction to shareholder primacy. That framing captures an important normative disagreement, but it leaves the theory’s institutional content underdeveloped. Firms and corporations are not neutral containers within which managers decide whose interests to consider. They are institutional arrangements constituted by formal and informal rules that allocate authority, voice, property claims, responsibilities, exposure to risk, and access to remedies.

The stakeholder question is therefore not only whether managers should care about non-shareholding groups. It is how institutions define relevant participants, organise their interdependence, structure conflicts, distribute decision rights, and adapt when existing rules cease to support viable cooperation.

The symposium’s organising question

How do institutions constitute stakeholder relationships, distribute authority and vulnerability among stakeholder groups, and evolve in response to conflict, uncertainty, power, and changing social and ecological conditions?

Original institutional economics offers powerful resources for this task. Veblen directs attention to evolving habits, technologies, power structures, and ceremonial valuations. Commons treats institutions as collective action that controls, liberates, and expands individual action, and analyses transactions as legally and socially constituted relations involving conflict, dependence, bargaining, and working rules. Later institutionalist work extends these insights through social provisioning, cumulative causation, institutional change, and the legal-economic nexus.

The symposium also welcomes contributions drawing on post-Keynesian, feminist, ecological, behavioural, humanistic, evolutionary, social, legal, comparative, polycentric, and organisational approaches. These traditions are relevant when they illuminate the design, operation, persistence, change, or comparative effects of identifiable institutions. The collection will not be a loose set of critiques of mainstream economics; it will be a focused institutional analysis of stakeholder governance.

Workshop theme: Decolonial Comparative Law and the Informal/Formal Economy

The exclusion of the many from access to, and the benefits of, means of production and resources has long been a colonial enterprise. Today, around 60% of the world’s labour force works in the informal economy. In legal terms, informality often translates into insecure social and economic rights – in short, precarity. At the same time, legal instruments designed to secure transactions, access to capital, and property are typically associated with the formal economy. Yet across Global South – or Global Majority – contexts, and increasingly in the Global North, participation in the formal economy does not guarantee stable economic rights.

This is paralleled by an exclusion of the informal economy within comparative law scholarship, which either ignores informality altogether or views it merely as a problem to be solved by law modelled after Global North law. This imbalance has limited the documentation of alternative legal instruments for human economies. Coloniality continues to sustain a narrow reading of how Global South and Indigenous societies structure their economic lives, including when they choose not to practise “economy” in a conventional sense. Acknowledging the heterogeneity of the informal economy requires attention to everyday legalities across both informal and formal work.

This workshop is not only interested in papers recommending or problematising formalisation initiatives. The main focus of the workshop is to take the informal economy seriously as a space of legality as such, in the context of legal pluralism. The organizers are looking for attempts to document, compare, and assess legal approaches – in formal and informal law – to the informal economy and the intersections between formal and informal economic life. The organizers welcome papers analysing how informal workers mobilise, transform, ignore, or reject state and non-state legal instruments in their economic lives, and examining how formal institutions engage with the informal sector.

Potential topics include, but are not limited to:

  • Informal cross-border trade, including commerce conducted by groups transcending state borders, regardless of their legality under state law.
  • Local and digital currencies created or used for noncolonial purposes.
  • Indigenous and customary economies, including their own value systems, exchange practices, and non-colonial monetary forms.
  • Ecofeminist, pastoralist, rural, and intentional communities (e.g. Auroville in India) as well as precolonial or other traditional modes of value creation (irrespective of the effective ancestry of the practice).
  • Labour rights in informal work, including economic dependence within and beyond the employer–employee relationship, dispute resolution practices, and collective organisation (e.g., trade unions, associations, cooperatives).
  • Microlending, alternative securities, and property rights as mechanisms for accessing capital.
  • Legal (mis)recognition of informal workers.
  • Migration and the (in)formal economy.
  • Globalisation and the informal labour serving the global supply chain.
  • Digital businesses, platform-based livelihoods (e.g. TikTok influencers, delivery and domestic workers hired online) and (in)formality.
  • State constraints on local economic sovereignty, including the spatial distribution and regulation of formal and informal economic activities.
  • Blurred lines between formal and informal economies: workers operating in both settings (e.g. civil servants’ side jobs; or ‘hustlers’, ‘débrouillards’, and ‘rebuscadores’).

If your research does not fit into any of these themes, the organizers still encourage you to submit a proposal. In general, the organizers invite papers that analyse and destabilise coloniality by examining, comparatively, the economic and legal imaginaries through which communities (typically, but not necessarily, in the Global South) define, practise, or decline to practise an economy beyond (or in spite of) coloniality.

item.title: Journal of Australian Political Economy: Special Issues on "Health Inequality" and "Political Economic Challenges"
item.description:
Deadline: 1 December 2026

JAPE No. 99 Special Issue: The Political Economy of Health Inequality

Over the preceding two decades, mainstream public health scholarship and political discourse has accorded increasing attention to health inequalities – both their pernicious effects on population health and well-being, and the need to devise policies to redress them. Most prominently, this focus has translated into an expansive literature addressing the social determinants of health (SDH), which recognises that health outcomes stem from myriad social factors beyond healthcare alone, and are not reducible to the products of economically organised medical science. Alternatively, in seeking to discern the complex determinants of human health and inequalities therein, this tradition highlights the importance of indicators of socio-economic status (SES), such as income, wealth, and education. SDH research predominantly isolates such indicators as a means to demonstrate their causal association with negative and/or positive health outcomes, thereby implying that securing the correct balance of SES indicators would precipitate more favourable societal and/or global health consequences.

Undoubtedly, the SDH literature has heightened analytical and public awareness of in-justices surrounding health and health delivery – a fact that was plainly evident during successive COVID waves, as the relations between inequality and ill-health became increasingly stark. Without pre-existing, broad institutional acceptance of the association of SES with health status among public health institutions, researchers, hospitals, and international organisations, discussions concerning inequality and COVID would not have occurred with such potency within media and governmental circles. Nevertheless, despite this important contribution in identifying a broad nexus of social factors shaping health outcomes, the SDH literature tends to disregard the ‘upstream’ social conditions and power structures that adversely affect health. That is, the tradition largely fails to progress further up the causal chain to address how the social determinants of poor health (such as inequality) are, themselves, determined by structural factors, such as class or the systemic imperative of capitalism toward perpetual capital accumulation. Inequality or socioeconomic status here simply refers to individuals or families who are higher or lower according to a particular metric without consideration of the antagonistic social relations between these groups.

Hence, while recognising the significance of SDH research in refocusing scholarly and political attention on social factors as the fulcrum of studies of health inequality, this special issue seeks to shift how we comprehend associations between inequality and health. It places the locus of causality not so much on socio-economic status, but rather on the embodied structural forces, power, and political struggles that bring about the proximate status of SES indicators in the first place. That is, it is concerned with the political economy of health inequalities – critically analysing the historically specific nexus of structures, processes, and social relations in contemporary capitalism that constitute the material and ideological conditions in which people live and work, and thereby engender particular individual and societal patterns of health, illness, and well-being.

Contributions to this special issue may address a range of questions on this theme, including (but not limited to):

  • Conceptualising health inequality via a political economy lens
  • Financialisation, the asset economy and health inequality
  • The corporatisation of Medicare, de-universalisation and growth of out-of-pocket health expenses
  • Climate change, planetary health and health inequalities
  • Food poverty and malnutrition
  • The co-constitutive relations between class, gender, sexual, racialised and spatial health inequalities
  • Corporate power, neoliberalism and the commodification of health
  • Methodological approaches to studying health inequality that address its structural causes
  • The contemporary welfare/workfare state and entrenching of poverty
  • Contesting the primarily techno-managerial framing of health inequalities in government policy
  • Capitalism, class struggle and health
  • Case-studies of health inequalities in Australia and/or globally
  • Policy and political opportunities to promote greater social justice – from universal basic services and greater healthcare universalism to structural and systemic change

Through consideration of such themes, the special issue will showcase the cutting-edge of contemporary scholarship on the political economy of health inequality. Papers should be between 6,000-8,000 words, and formatted using the Harvard style.

item.title: Review of Political Economy and Economia e Sociedade: Joint Symposium on "What should Central Banks do?"
item.description:
Deadline: 15 August 2026

What Should Central Banks Do?

Central banks were first designed to deal with financial instability and to give economic and financial support to governments by funding public debt. This was their primary raison d’être. The earliest institutions, like the Bank of England (1694), were established specifically to finance military conflicts and manage national treasuries. Later, banks like the U.S. Federal Reserve (1913) were created as “lenders of last resort” to stop bank panics and standardize currency. As time went on, however, central banks were called upon to assume additional tasks, notably the responsibility for keeping inflation ‘low and stable’ and for addressing unemployment.

Viewed from the periphery, this question cannot be separated from the hierarchical nature of the global monetary and financial system. That hierarchy shapes even central banks' ‘core’ objectives, so what is at stake is less the addition of new mandates than the degree of monetary sovereignty peripheral capitalist states possess in the first place.

Today, as research has progressed and new economic challenges have arisen, central banks are being called upon once more — from various ideological sides — to address issues of inequality and the environment, and to participate in quantitative easing for the people.

But are central banks able to address all these issues? Or, more importantly, should they? In the end, are we not asking central banks to do too much? Should central banks address income inequality? Should they address ecological problems, and, above all, should they distribute money to the general public?

It is of course one thing to recognize that monetary policy has distributive or ecological consequences, but asking central banks to address these issues is a matter of great debate. Does this fall into the mainstream trap of accepting ‘monetary policy dominance’, as coined by Rochon and Setterfield? Are central banks equipped to deal with these additional problems, or should they be relegated to fiscal policy?

Such is the question posed by this joint symposium between the Review of Political Economy and Economia e Sociedade. Our aim is to publish a total of twenty articles across the two journals, asking the important question of what central banks should do today.

The Journal of Critical Economics announces a call for papers for its semi-monographic issue for the second half of 2027 on ‘Transformations of contemporary capitalism: neoliberalism, authoritarianism and the war economy’.

Editors

  • Aurelia Mañé Estrada (UB)
  • Albert Recio Andreu (UAB)

For decades, analysis of capitalist economies has focused on neoliberalism as the emerging order that emerged from the crisis of the 1970s, centred on deregulation, financialisation and globalisation. However, this project — which has always been marked by social resistance and differing national trajectories — has shown clear limitations since the 2007 crisis, following which austerity policies reinforced inequalities and weakened the material foundations of democracy.

Neoliberalism has operated not only as an economic policy, but also as an institutional project and a rationale that reshapes the conditions of democracy, fostering processes of de-democratisation, technocratisation and authoritarianism. In this context, rising inequality, the ecological crisis and the transformations of digital capitalism are combined with the rise of the far right and a growing structural convergence between neoliberalism and new forms of fascism.

At the same time, we are witnessing significant shifts in the role of the state and in global regulation: directed reindustrialisation, a crisis of multilateralism, geopolitical tensions and the intensification of armed conflicts, and a slowdown in ecological transition policies… Within this framework, we are seeing a return to active fiscal policies and the emergence of a possible ‘war-time Keynesianism’, in which defence spending acts as a driver of demand, innovation and productive reorganisation.

Whilst inequalities continue to grow and affect the living conditions of an increasing proportion of the population, even in the dominant countries, new types of business have emerged which wield significant economic power through their control of the central networks of the new digital economy. The debate over how to characterise this new form of capitalism is ongoing, with concepts such as ‘surveillance capitalism’ or ‘techno-feudalism’ being put forward in an attempt to capture the nature of a new model that is more predatory than its predecessor. At the same time, driven by the United States, we are witnessing the dismantling of plurinational institutions and a resurgence of imperial and military tensions. A key aspect of this process is the weakening of policies designed to tackle ecological problems. Growing inequalities, the ecological crisis, imperialist conflicts and the rise of a far right that imposes policies aimed at dismantling rights paint a dramatic picture.

The aim of this special issue is to analyse these transformations, their causes and their direction, taking into account both the continuities and the breaks with historical neoliberalism.

item.title: Evolutionary and Institutional Economics Review: Special Issue on "Japanese Capitalism Evolving with Uncertain Institutional Transformation and Growth Regimes"
item.description:
Deadline: 31 December 2026

Associate Editors: Hiroshi Nishi (Ritsumeikan University), Yuji Harada (Setsunan University)

Guest Editor: Kazuhiro Okuma (Tokai University)

Publication: The April 2027 Issue

Since the collapse of the asset price bubble in the early 1990s, Japanese capitalism has experienced more than three decades of sluggish growth while repeatedly confronting major domestic and international crises. During this prolonged low-growth period, Japan appears to have undergone profound structural and institutional transformations. These include depopulation and population ageing; the expansion of non-regular employment and persistent wage stagnation; the financialisation of the non-corporate sector and its increasing retention of earnings; accelerating digitalisation and AI adoption amid advancing platformisation; the reorganisation of global and regional value chains alongside sluggish domestic capital investment and a sharp rise in overseas investment; and the growing urgency of environmental and energy transitions.

The recent shift from persistent deflation to inflation further suggests the possible emergence of a new phase in the Japanese economy. At the same time, the weakening of the social security system and the accumulation of substantial government debt remain major concerns. Against this backdrop, Japan’s pre-global financial crisis export-led growth regime has effectively collapsed, while persistent trade deficits combined with income surpluses have become the new normal.

Taken together, these cumulative transformations raise a central question: how have market mechanisms, institutional coordination, and government policies evolved, and can they provide a coherent basis for a new growth regime under the dynamic evolution of global and regional production networks?At the same time, they revive longstanding concerns in evolutionary and institutional political economy: how institutional forms shape economic behaviours and their coordination; how, together with market mechanisms, they stabilise or destabilise capitalist economies; how coherent accumulation and growth regimes are generated; and how crises emerge when such coherence erodes, prompting structural transformation and new modes of régulation (institutional coordination).

Building on the intellectual foundations of evolutionary and institutional political economy, the varieties of capitalism, and Régulation theory (Boyer and Yamada, eds. 2000), prior special issues of Evolutionary and Institutional Economics Review have elucidated institutional coordination, the characteristics of Japan’s growth regime, and its embeddedness within varieties of Asian capitalism until the early 2000s (Uemura and Harada 2016; Boyer et al. 2018). Yet, particularly in the post–global financial crisis era marked by the transformations outlined above, the trajectory of the Japanese economy remains unclear. It is therefore fair to say that Japanese capitalism is evolving through uncertain institutional transformations and fragile growth regimes amid the dynamic restructuring of global production networks.

This special issue “Japanese capitalism evolving with uncertain institutional transformation and growth regime” seeks to elucidate the transformation of Japanese capitalism during the prolonged low-growth era. Specifically, it aims to:

  • Clarify how multi-level institutional structures, including the wage–labour nexus, market–firm nexus, industrial structures, monetary and financial systems, and policy regimes, have evolved in Japan under global and regional production networks.
  • Specify the nature of Japan’s growth regime and its capacity to achieve resilient development in the face of multiple shocks.
  • Advance empirical research in contemporary evolutionary and institutional political economy through in-depth analyses of Japanese capitalism.

To these ends, the editors invite contributions addressing the following themes related to the Japanese economy:

  1. Institutional coordination and market adjustment under the reorganisation of global and regional value chains and heightened geopolitical uncertainty.
  2. Complementarities and hierarchical relations among institutional domains such as labour markets, corporate governance, industrial organisation, financial systems, welfare regimes, and environmental and energy policies.
  3. Transformations in firm behaviour, production systems, and industrial structures in the era of AI diffusion and platformisation, including multi-level approaches aligned with recent Régulationist advances (e.g. meso-level analyses of sectors, value chains, and technological trajectories).
  4. The evolution and reconfiguration of Japan’s growth regime, with particular attention to demand and productivity dynamics, distributional patterns, demographic pressures, and ecological constraints.
  5. Empirical and historical studies drawing on macro-level, firm-level, or industry-level data, as well as regional perspectives or international comparative datasets.
  6. Comparative analyses situating Japan within the broader landscape of global varieties of capitalism.

Money structures economic life and global markets. Rather than functioning merely as a tool for exchange and trade, money has become a master that is shaping priorities and guiding decision-making in ever more realms. Although money is ostensibly a human artefact, it has come to play quasi‑agentive roles by preconfiguring markets and consumption patterns in ways that generate negative consequences for the climate and ecological systems. As the creation of money through credit pushes economies to continue growing, and as the conventional money form itself obscures the socioecological relations that underpin it, money, monetary institutions and valuation practices are based on and influence patterns of extraction, carbon emissions, and environmental degradation. At the same time, emerging ideas and experiments in alternative forms of money and monetary design raise new questions about how economic coordination might better align with planetary limits and climate stabilization goals.

The organizers invite submissions for a two-day academic conference exploring the relationships between money, monetary systems and ecological processes. The conference aims to bring together scholars from environmental studies, sociology, political science, geography, anthropology, STS and related fields to critically examine how money shapes ecological processes and outcomes, as well as how alternative monetary arrangements might support more sustainable socioeconomic futures. The organizers welcome theoretical, empirical, and interdisciplinary contributions addressing topics such as:

  • The ecological implications of conventional forms of monetary and financial systems
  • Monetary policy, central banking and climate change
  • Financialization, indebtedness, and ecological transformation

  • Alternative and complementary currencies

item.title: Social Studies of Economics after Neoliberalism? (Berlin, December 2026)
item.description:
Deadline: July 15, 2026

3–4 December, 2026 | Berlin, Germany

The Social Studies of Economics (SSE) is an interdisciplinary field that examines the role of economists, economics and economic knowledge in society. Over the past decade, SSE has consolidated as a distinct research area, focusing on the influence and performativity of economics — how economic theories and models actively shape social realities — and the intellectual and institutional structure of economics, including its homogeneity and epistemic authority. Key debates in SSE include

  • the influence of economic imaginaries on policymaking and public discourse
  • the role of economists as powerful experts
  • the mechanisms of economic knowledge dissemination in academia and beyond
  • the contribution of economic reasoning to the emergence, perpetuation and transformation of neoliberalism.

However, political-economic developments over the past 15 years and the mutually dependent disruptions associated with economic, political, social and ecological crises suggest that neoliberalism, at least as an economic policy paradigm, has come to an end. While several political activists and scientists argue for a social-ecological transformation as the progressive successor of neoliberalism, regressive alternatives — comprising right-wing populism, techno-libertarianism, and authoritarian ideologies — are gaining strength in the emerging era of post-neoliberalism. Economic knowledge and imaginaries, as central frameworks of thought that shape how societies perceive and organize economic realities, play a crucial role in these developments. These imaginaries not only underpin the rhetoric of these movements but also reveal fractures within traditional economic thought. For instance, the tension between economic liberalism, which emphasizes progress and market-driven innovation, and regressive ideologies, which often advocate protectionism, nationalism, or anti-globalization, highlights the contested nature of economic reasoning in contemporary society. At the same time, there are resemblances and mutual reinforcements between market-radical and right-wing concepts on several levels, including the discursive construction of dichotomous world views and an implicitly derogative conceptualization of masses. The project of socio-ecological transformation also has diverse connections to economic knowledge. On the one hand, technocratic "green growth" approaches rely on empirical evidence from academic economics; on the other hand, some voices call for a left-wing populism that challenges traditional economic liberalism as well as the epistemic authority of academic economics.

These developments challenge SSE and its established perspectives on economists, economics and economic knowledge. The workshop seeks to discuss how SSE can address recent societal and political trends in research on the role of economists, economics and economic knowledge in society, exploring the political-economic, ideological, epistemic and societal characteristics of a contested post-neoliberal era and their implications for SSE and related fields such as Science and Technology Studies (STS).

Contributions should address questions such as:

  • To what extent do we face the end — or yet another crisis — of neoliberalism and neoliberal economic reasoning?
  • How does economic reasoning relate to the rise of regressive ideologies? What is the economic reasoning behind concrete regressive imaginaries?
  • What is the role of economic reasoning and economic experts in debates about socio-ecological transformation?
  • What actors and institutions contribute to new economic imaginaries?
  • How do these developments reflect broader shifts in the relationship between economic knowledge production and societal values?
  • And how do they contribute to the further marginalisation of distinct groups of economists along the dimensions of paradigm, gender, ethnicity and class?

Travel costs, accommodation, and conference meals are covered for all participants, thanks to support from the VolkswagenStiftung.

Abstracts should be submitted to rouven.reinke@uni-hamburg.de, lukas.baeuerle@jku.at, and stephan.puehringer@jku.at.
